prompt.context: Stefan Lessard, the CEO of a large conglomerate, finds a once-in-a-lifetime deal and buys a satellite at a heavily discounted price. He can keep it or sell it today for a profit.
prompt.question: What questions could you ask to gain critical information? And what is the best road to profits for DMB Satellite?

clarifying_info.q: How much did the satellite cost to acquire?
What is the market value of the satellite today?
What are the repair and maintenance costs?
clarifying_info.a: Negligible. The satellite is in good condition.

clarifying_info.q: Has the satellite been launched yet?
clarifying_info.a: No, it is still in the box and needs to be launched if the company decides to keep it.

clarifying_info.q: How long can the satellite be used after launch?
clarifying_info.a: 3 years, after which it becomes obsolete with $0 resale value and non-functional.
$10 million for high orbit launch; $8 million for low orbit launch.

clarifying_info.q: What is the difference between low orbit and high orbit satellites?
clarifying_info.a: Low orbit satellites transmit data between two points 3,000–5,000 miles apart, used by corporations to transmit data in batches; signal is subject to high interference so not used for continuous transmission. High orbit satellites are used for continuous real-time transmission where signal quality is critical; primary application is live global television broadcasting.

clarifying_info.q: What is the life expectancy of the satellite?
clarifying_info.a: 5 years (it needs to be replaced in 5 years as it becomes obsolete).

Two segments: (1) Large corporations for data transmission — use is short and intermittent, allowing multiple clients. (2) News broadcasters and telecom companies for voice/video transmission — require 24-hour global coverage, limiting to only one client.
Leasing satellite capacity is a good option but not available in this case.

clarifying_info.q: What revenue can we expect from low orbit customers?
clarifying_info.a: Year 1 customers pay $50,000/month; Year 2 customers pay $30,000/month; Year 3 customers pay $20,000/month. Prices for contracts signed in Year 1 fall to new rates in Year 2. 80% of customers from a given year will remain the following year.

clarifying_info.q: How many customers can we expect each year in the low orbit scenario?
clarifying_info.a: 50 new customers in Year 1, 40 new customers in Year 2, 30 new customers in Year 3.

clarifying_info.q: What revenue can we expect from a high orbit customer?
clarifying_info.a: $2,500,000 per month. This is a specialized market with only one potential customer ready to sign.

framework: Identify the three strategic options: (1) Sell satellite today, (2) Launch low orbit — multiple corporate data clients, (3) Launch high orbit — single voice/video client
Quantify upfront costs for each option (acquisition cost as sunk cost, launch costs)
Calculate total revenues over the 3-year operating life for options 2 and 3
Calculate pre-tax profit for each option
Assess qualitative factors: customer concentration risk, capital access, market dynamics
Deliver a recommendation with supporting rationale and risks

questions.prompt: Option 1: If DMB sells the satellite today, what is the profit?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates recognize the $10M acquisition cost is a sunk cost. Profit = market value today minus sunk cost (sunk cost should not reduce the opportunity value, but the case frames profit as $35M pre-tax).

math.setup: Selling price = $35M; acquisition cost = $10M (sunk cost). Pre-tax profit = $35M.
steps: Profit = $35M (market value) - $0 incremental cost to sell = $35M pre-tax

questions.prompt: Option 2: Calculate the total pre-tax profit from operating the satellite in low orbit (multiple corporate clients) over 3 years.
questions.guidance: Candidate must track cohorts: 50 new clients in Y1, 40 new in Y2, 30 new in Y3. Y1 clients earn $50K/month, Y2 clients earn $30K/month, Y3 clients earn $20K/month. Existing clients renew at new (lower) rates. 80% retention rate means Y1 cohort of 50 becomes 40 in Y2, and 40 in Y2 becomes 32 in Y3. Launch cost = $8M.

math.setup:
Revenue by cohort and year; launch cost = $8M.
Y1: 50 clients x $50,000/month x 12 months
Y2: 50 retained clients (50*80%=40) at $30K/month x 12, plus 40 new clients at $30K/month x 12
Y3: 40 Y1-cohort retained (40*80%=32) at $20K/month x 12, plus 40 Y2-cohort retained (40*80%=32) at $20K/month x 12, plus 30 new clients at $20K/month x 12
steps: Y2 revenue from Y1 cohort (40 clients at $30K): 40 x $30,000 x 12 = $14,400,000
Y2 revenue from Y2 new cohort (40 clients at $30K): 40 x $30,000 x 12 = $14,400,000
Y3 revenue: 32 retained Y1 clients + 32 retained Y2 clients + 30 new clients, all at $20K x 12
math.answer: Approximately $77,200,000 pre-tax profit (casebook solution: ~$73,360,000 after full cohort tracking)

questions.prompt: Option 3: Calculate the total pre-tax profit from operating the satellite in high orbit (single voice/video client) over 3 years.
questions.guidance: One client at $2.5M/month for 36 months. Launch cost = $10M. Simple calculation.

math.setup: 1 client x $2,500,000/month x 36 months; launch cost = $10,000,000
math.answer: $80,000,000 pre-tax profit (casebook: $85,000,000 pre-tax per summary; $80M per detailed calc)

questions.prompt: Compare all three options and identify which generates the highest profit.
questions.guidance: Option 1 = $35M; Option 2 = ~$73-77M; Option 3 = ~$80-85M. Option 3 generates the highest profit but comes with significant risk. Candidate should flag that access to capital for purchase and launch must be verified.

math.answer: Option 3 has highest profit, but risk and capital access must be considered

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key risks and considerations for each option?

categories.name: Option 1 – Sell Today
ideas: Immediate liquidity with no execution risk
Opportunity cost: $35M proceeds vs $77–85M from operating
Sunk cost of $10M acquisition is irrelevant to this decision
Does DMB have better investment opportunities for the $35M?
Satellite market value is unusually high ($35M vs $10M cost); unlikely to find another deal like this

categories.name: Option 2 – Low Orbit Multi-Client
ideas: Diversified client base reduces customer concentration risk
Revenue declines each year due to increasing competition
Customer retention of 80% creates revenue uncertainty
Requires access to $8M launch capital upfront
More operationally complex — managing many client relationships

categories.name: Option 3 – High Orbit Single Client
ideas: Single client creates extreme concentration risk
Client bankruptcy or contract cancellation would eliminate all revenue
Very limited customer pool in this specialized market
Requires access to $10M launch capital upfront

recommendation: Option 2 (low orbit, multiple clients) appears to be the optimal choice, balancing strong profitability (~$73–77M) with diversified revenue across many clients
Option 3 yields the highest profit (~$80–85M) but the single-client concentration risk and limited customer pool make it a high-risk bet
Option 1 should only be considered if DMB lacks access to capital for the launch costs or has a superior alternative use of the $35M proceeds
risks: Option 3: Single client could go bankrupt, renegotiate aggressively, or be lost — all revenue disappears
Option 2: Competitive pressure drives prices down year over year; 20% annual churn reduces revenue trajectory
Both operating options require capital access for launch ($8M or $10M) — must verify DMB has this
The satellite becomes fully obsolete after 3 years with zero residual value
next_steps: Verify DMB has access to sufficient capital for the selected launch option
Conduct due diligence on prospective customers — creditworthiness, contract terms, lock-in provisions
If pursuing Option 3, negotiate multi-year contract with strong termination penalties to reduce single-client risk
If pursuing Option 2, build a sales pipeline to exceed the 50/40/30 customer projections and offset price erosion
